headline: Bay water runs hot, fluke slide to the inlet, and the new moon sets up a sunset striper window
subhead: Jamaica Bay's flats are cooking past 78 degrees — the real action this week is where moving water meets the heat.
body_markdown:
Last week the bay basically turned into a bathtub. Flat calm, sun beating down, and the shallow flats off Canarsie and up in the back creeks climbed into the high 70s — I heard 78, 79 degrees from a couple guys running temp gauges off Beach Channel. That's warm enough that fluke don't want to sit still on the flats anymore. They get lethargic, oxygen gets thin, and they slide toward whatever's got current running through it — the inlet mouth, the bridge channels, anywhere water's actually moving and staying a touch cooler. That's exactly what I saw happen this week. The bay bite that was solid back in May and June has thinned out on the shallow stuff and pushed hard toward Rockaway Inlet and the ocean side.

Here's what's coming: we're building toward a new moon on the 10th, which means spring tides stacking up through the weekend, peaking around the 11th through the 13th. Bigger swings, stronger current, and — this is the part I like — the PM flood is going to line up almost perfectly with sunset those evenings. That's the first evening window like this since the June full moon, and it's the kind of setup that gets bass moving and feeding hard right at last light instead of just picking at bait in the dark. If you've got one evening to fish this week, Friday through Monday at the Marine Parkway Bridge on that building flood, right into dusk, is where I'd be.

Stripers have been working the bridge pilings on the outgoing, same as always this time of year, but with the new moon current building, the outgoing's going to run harder and push more bait past those pilings than it has in weeks. I'm throwing a white bucktail, an ounce and a half, with a white curly-tail trailer, and working the downcurrent seam off the pilings — that's where the ambush happens, not right up against the concrete. Guys are also doing well with darker swimming plugs at dusk when the light gets low. Sizes have been schoolie-heavy, 18 to 24 inches, but there's been enough mid-20s mixed in that a slot fish isn't a surprise. Nobody's telling me about a run of true keepers yet, but with that sunset flood window coming, I wouldn't be shocked if this week changes that.

Bluefish have shown up with some teeth on them. Breezy Point and the Rockaway Beach surf line have had blitzes in the early morning — bunker peanuts and silversides getting run right up into the wash, gulls diving, the whole show. If you catch it, metal is the move: Deadly Dicks, Kastmasters, anything you can chuck far and retrieve fast through the mess. Snapper blues are also thick in the bay proper right now if you've got kids who want steady action off Canarsie Pier — small stuff, but it keeps a rod bent.

Fluke is the one where I have to be straight with you: the bay bite is inconsistent right now, and it's because of that heat I mentioned. I fished the flats off Canarsie two days this week and it was slow going, a few short fish and one keeper over three hours. But guys working the Rockaway Inlet mouth and the deeper cuts along Beach Channel are doing noticeably better — 15 to 25 feet, drifting the outgoing with white or chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, tipped with a strip of squid if you've got it. There's upwelled ocean water pushing in on that outgoing tide that's running cooler than the bay, and that's exactly where the bigger fish have relocated. If you're set on fluke this week, fish the inlet and the ocean-side drifts off Breezy Point, not the shallow flats. That's not where the fish are living right now.

Porgies have actually been a bright spot inside the bay — structure around the Cross Bay Bridge and the rock piles near Canarsie Pier have given up decent numbers on bloodworm and clam, moderate depth, nothing fancy needed. If you want a stress-free evening with a bucket of bait and a simple high-low rig, that's your play.

Weakfish — I'll be honest, I haven't heard a single real report out of the bay or the inlet despite the warm water. The temperature's been there for weeks now and it just hasn't translated into fish showing up. I wouldn't plan a trip around them right now.

Looking ahead, that new moon spring tide building into the weekend is the story. Bigger current, more bait getting flushed through the inlet and past the bridge, and a sunset flood window Friday through Monday that's the best alignment we've had in a month. If I only had one evening, I'd be at Marine Parkway working the outgoing into that flood, switching over to bucktails as the light dies. Backup plan if the bass don't show — head to the inlet mouth and drift bucktails for fluke on that same tide change, because that bite's been the more reliable one lately even if it's not blowing up. Keep an eye on the ocean side too — bluefish have been aggressive enough in the surf that a dawn trip to Breezy Point could pay off on its own, blitz or no blitz.
